newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: U.S. says Savimbi still wants peace. [CORRECTED 07:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Savimbi still wants peace. [CORRECTED 07:35 GMT]

text.p: The United States believes Jonas Savimbi, leader of the former rebel group UNITA, is still committed to peace in Angola but has warned that if he again chooses war the international community will not stand by him, officials say. (Corrects to make clear Savimbi is still UNITA's leader).
Secretary of State Warren Christopher, at the end of a five-nation African tour, wanted to meet Savimbi in Luanda, the Angolan capital, on Monday to discuss the country's threatened peace process.

But Savimbi, who once depended on Washington and white South Africa to finance his guerrilla war against the then-Marxist government in Luanda, turned down the request, citing personal security concerns if he came to the capital.
Christopher rejected Savimbi's suggestion that the two men meet in another country or at the UNITA leader's base camp because it would "send the wrong signal", U.S. officials said.
The U.S. secretary will stop in Luanda anyway to meet President Eduardo dos Santos.

U.S. officials reject Savimbi's personal security concerns about Luanda and say his refusal to meet Christopher this week and African regional leaders last week reinforces reservations about his commitment to the peace process.
"I think we're still prepared to give him the benefit of the doubt but we would like very much to see concrete manifestations, again, of that commitment," one official said.

Washington says new punitive action against UNITA is premature. But if it becomes clear Savimbi has forsaken the peace process, sanctions and a withdrawal of U.N. peacekeeping troops from Angola must be weighed, the official said.

"There's no appetite for (renewed) war. I think Savimbi knows that and wants peace. I think he knows that if he were to choose war again there would be no sanctuary for him in the inernational community. There would be zero tolerance."
The U.N. Security Council on Friday threatened sanctions against UNITA and extended the U.N.'s 7,200-strong peacekeeping mission in Angola for two months only.

But it rejected demands from southern African countries to automatically begin sanctions next month unless UNITA (the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola) complied with peace accords that ended two decades of civil warfare.

Instead, the resolution, drafted by the United States, Russia and Portugal, says the council would consider bans against UNITA's trade in the oil- and mineral-rich country if no progress has been made by November 20.

This could include preventing travel and freezing bank accounts abroad. The council threatened such action in 1993 but never followed through. It has imposed an oil and arms embargo against UNITA but has had trouble enforcing it.

The U.N. says UNITA delayed integrating 26,000 fighters into a national army with its former enemies, interfered with U.N. peacekeepers and helicopters in key areas and relinquished only old arms for those guerrillas being demobilised.
UNITA is now delaying the peace process, although at other times the government could be blamed, officials said.
Savimbi may regret refusing to attend the regional leaders' meeting in Luanda and meet Christopher. Officials said he is extending "selective olive branches" through private channels.

The U.N. peacekeeping operation in Angola, its largest remaining mission, will be renewed for two months until December 20 to maintain pressure on both parties. But it is expected to be renewed until February 8, the target for ending the operation.

The U.N. is helping to implement a 1994 accord ending nearly 20 years of civil war between the Angolan government and UNITA. In the Cold War, UNITA forces were bolstered by South Africa's apartheid government with U.S. acquiescence while its opponents were helped by Cuban troops backed by the then Soviet Union.
